Searching Algorithms26.1Using lists or arrays to store data helps us organise large amounts of related data. To find a record in the list that is the same as the target value, we need to perform a search. Whether the items in the list are sorted will also affect the design and efficiency of the algorithm. This chapter will discuss the design and efficiency of different search algorithms.
Binary search20B4. Since the item is larger than the target value, it means that the target value can only appear in the first half of the search range.
Binary search21B5. Narrow the search range again and compare the item in the middle.
Binary search22B6. Since the item is smaller than the target value, it means that the target value can only appear in the second half of the search range.
Binary search23B7. The search is finally narrowed down to just one item. If this item is the same as the target value, the search ends. Otherwise, the target value does not exist in the list.

Binary search28BBinary search assumes that the items in a list have been sorted and starts searching from the middle of the list. After each comparison, even if the item is not the same as the target value, the search range can be reduced by half.
Binary search29BThe worst case is that the target value is stored in the last item in the list or does not exist in it. That is, after the ith iteration, only one item remains in the search range.

Linear search3AThe easiest way to know if the target value exists in the list is to search the list from the beginning, i.e. start from index 0, then go through index 1, index 2 and so on until you reach the last index in the list or find the target value. This algorithm is called linear search. It is often used to search unsorted lists.

Sorting Algorithms486.3As its name suggests, sorting means arranging a series of data in ascending or descending order. We often need to sort data for different purposes. For example, in a spreadsheet that stores the marks of 100 students, the marks are sorted from highest to lowest.

Sorting Algorithms496.3Sorting is also relevant to binary search, which we have learnt earlier. Binary search helps us find the target value quickly, but this algorithm is only applicable to sorted lists.

Linear search5AIf the target value entered exists in the list, e.g. “50”, the final output of the program will be True;  If the target value entered does not exist in the list, e.g. “100”, the final output of the program will be False instead.

Selection sort50ASelection sort is based on linear search. The algorithm repeatedly carries out linear search in the unsorted part of the list in order to find the maximum or minimum value. Then, this value is swapped with the first item of the unsorted list so as to set up the sorted part of the list. This process is repeated until all list items have been sorted.

Selection sort51AThe following Python program uses selection sort to sort list mark in descending order:	for i in range(0, len(mark)):		max_index = i		for j in range(i+1, len(mark)):			if mark[j] > mark[max_index]:				max_index = j		temp = mark[i]		mark[i] = mark[max_index]		mark[max_index] = temp
Selection sort52A1. Firstly, perform linear search on the list to find the maximum value.
Selection sort53A1. Firstly, perform linear search on the list to find the maximum value.
Selection sort54A2. Swap the maximum value with the first item of the list.
Selection sort55AThis divides the sorted and unsorted parts of the list.
Selection sort56A3. Then, perform linear search on the unsorted part to find the maximum value.
Selection sort57A4. Swap the maximum value with the first item of the unsorted list.
Selection sort58AThis adds an item to the sorted list.
Selection sort59A5. Repeat the above operations of linear search and swapping.

Insertion sort70BInsertion sort divides the list into the sorted and unsorted parts, then one of the list items in the unsorted part (key value) is inserted into the correct position in the sorted part of the list. This process is repeated until all list items have been sorted.
Insertion sort71BThe following list mark stores the exam marks of seven students, as shown below:Suppose that the list is to be sorted in descending order:

Insertion sort72BThe following Python program uses insertion sort to sort list mark in descending order:	for i in range(1, len(mark)):		key = mark[i]		j = i-1		while j >= 0 and key > mark[j]:			mark[j+1] = mark[j]			j = j – 1		mark[j+1] = key
Insertion sort73B1. Firstly, set apart the first item of the list as the sorted part. Then, take out the first item of the unsorted part (known as “key value”).

Insertion sort74B2. To find the correct position for inserting the key value, compare the key value with each list item in the sorted part on the left. If that item is smaller than the key value, move it backwards
Insertion sort75B3. Since all the list items in the sorted part have been compared, the key value should eventually be inserted into the first position of the list.

Insertion sort76B4. Now, an item is added to the sorted section. Similarly, take out the first item of the unsorted part. Compare it with each list item in the sorted part on the left. If that item is smaller than the key value, move it backwards.
Insertion sort77B5. When a larger item is found, stop moving the items. Here is the position where the key value should be inserted into the list.
Insertion sort78B6. Repeat the above operations.
Insertion sort79B7. Repeat until all list items have been sorted.

Bubble sort90CBubble sort starts from the first item of the list and compares an item with its adjacent item. If the two items are in the wrong positions, they will be swapped.
Bubble sort91CThe following list mark stores the exam marks of seven students, as shown below:Suppose that the list is to be sorted in descending order.

Bubble sort92CThe following Python program writes the algorithm of bubble sort:	for i in range(0, len(mark)-1):		for j in range(0, len(mark)-1-i):			if mark[j] < mark[j+1]:				temp = mark[j]				mark[j] = mark[j+1]				mark[j+1] = temp
Bubble sort93C1. Starting from the leftmost item of the list, compare two adjacent list items.
Bubble sort94C1. If the value on the left is smaller, swap the two items.
Bubble sort95C2. After the above operation has been completed on the whole list, the smallest value will move (rise) to the last item. This divides the list into the sorted and unsorted parts.
Bubble sort96C3. Starting from the leftmost item in the unsorted part, compare two adjacent list items.
Bubble sort97C3. If the value on the left is smaller, swap the two items.
Bubble sort98C4. After the above operation has been completed once again, the second smallest value will move (rise) to the second last item. This adds one item to the sorted part.
Bubble sort99C5. Repeat until all list items have been sorted.
